clinicalPearls: The classic triad reflects somatostatin's inhibitory actions: diabetes mellitus, gallstones, and steatorrhoea with weight loss
The full syndrome is uncommon; many tumours are found incidentally or present with mass effect rather than florid hormonal features
Pancreatic tumours more often produce the complete inhibitory syndrome, whereas duodenal or periampullary lesions may present with obstructive jaundice or bleeding
Diabetes tends to be mild because somatostatin suppresses both insulin and glucagon
Gallstones arise from reduced gallbladder contractility and diminished cholecystokinin-driven emptying
Steatorrhoea results from inhibition of pancreatic exocrine secretion and bile flow
A markedly elevated plasma somatostatin supports the diagnosis, and somatostatin-receptor imaging aids localisation and staging
Duodenal tumours may be associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, and pancreatic lesions with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
reference.pathophysiology: Somatostatinoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumour of pancreatic delta cells or duodenal somatostatin-producing cells. Excess somatostatin exerts broad inhibitory effects across the gastroenteropancreatic axis, suppressing insulin and glucagon (producing mild diabetes), reducing gallbladder motility and cholecystokinin action (favouring gallstone formation), and dampening pancreatic exocrine and biliary secretion (causing fat malabsorption and steatorrhoea). Many tumours are large and metastatic at diagnosis, and periampullary lesions may declare themselves through local obstruction rather than hormonal excess.
additionalDifferentials: Other functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours such as glucagonoma or VIPoma
Coeliac disease or other malabsorptive states
additionalInvestigations: Somatostatin-receptor imaging such as gallium DOTATATE positron emission tomography
Cross-sectional imaging and endoscopic ultrasound to localise and stage the tumour
Assessment of glycaemic status and pancreatic exocrine function
Screening for neurofibromatosis type 1 and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 where relevant
redFlags: Obstructive jaundice from a periampullary tumour
Progressive weight loss and malnutrition from severe steatorrhoea
Gastrointestinal haemorrhage from a duodenal lesion
Features suggesting an inherited tumour syndrome
reference.prognosis: Outlook depends heavily on stage; small, completely resected tumours can be cured, but a large proportion are advanced with hepatic or nodal metastases at diagnosis, when surgical resection and somatostatin analogues aim to control disease and symptoms rather than cure.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because the full inhibitory triad is often incomplete or subtle
Attributing the mild diabetes and gallstones to common coincidental disease
Overlooking a periampullary tumour presenting purely with obstructive symptoms
Failing to screen for associated neurofibromatosis type 1 or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
Assuming resectability without adequate somatostatin-receptor and cross-sectional staging
management: Complete surgical resection by enucleation or pancreaticoduodenectomy is the mainstay and potentially curative for localised tumours
Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide or lanreotide to control hormonal symptoms and slow progression in advanced disease
Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy with lutetium-177 DOTATATE for progressive somatostatin-receptor-positive metastatic disease
Manage syndrome components with insulin or oral hypoglycaemic agents for diabetes and pancreatic enzyme replacement for steatorrhoea
Cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones, often performed at the time of tumour resection
Liver-directed therapy such as embolisation or metastasectomy for hepatic metastases
Screen for associated neurofibromatosis type 1 and MEN1, with referral for genetic counselling where relevant
